title: Looking back
hook: 331 days ago you breathed at the bottom of the hill

segments.voice: Yesterday: Franklin's little book. Your line was my own data. Did you write your first line in the log? What, how long, how you felt? Day three hundred twenty-five.

Halfway up a real hill, there's a moment worth waiting for. You've been staring at your feet for an hour, at the next rock, the next root. It seems you've gone nowhere. Then you stop, turn around, and there it is: the parking lot is a speck, the town is a map, and the path you walked winds all the way up to where you're standing. You didn't feel yourself climbing. You just kept putting one foot down. That's where we are. Six days from now, year one ends. So this last week is a lookout. Today we turn around. Today: looking back.
screen: `STARING AT YOUR FEET.` → `THEN YOU TURN AROUND.` → `THE PATH, ALL THE WAY UP.`

segments.voice: First, the bottom of the hill. On day one, the very first thing we did was breathe. One breath, with the bell, and the discovery that in Latin, Greek and Hebrew, one word can mean both breath and spirit. Your line was someone is in there, say hi. Second, the camps. Then came the stories: Marcus arguing with his blanket, Nasruddin looking for his key under the lamp, Zhuangzi and the butterfly, Hillel on one foot. Then the practices: breath, the evening review, the view from above, the digital sabbath, sunset. Then the text: Rumi's reed flute, with Marcus Aurelius beside him. And this last camp, the depths: visits to seven traditions as a guest, the Stoics up close, and the science of practice. Third, why looking back is its own practice. Kierkegaard, the walker from four days ago, wrote in his journal that life can only be understood looking backward, but has to be lived looking forward. When you're in the middle of a day, you can't see the shape. From up here, you can. Fourth, how to look back well. Not to grade yourself. Some days you skipped, and some weeks the practice was one breath in a parked car. That counts. The habit study told us one missed day doesn't reset anything. Look back the way you'd look at a friend's photos from a long trip: with curiosity, and a little wonder that they went so far. Notice what changed, even a little. Notice what didn't. Both are data. Both belong to the climb.
screen: `DAY ONE: ONE BREATH.` · `STORIES, PRACTICES, THE TEXT, THE DEPTHS.` · `UNDERSTOOD BACKWARD, LIVED FORWARD.` · `NOT A GRADE: A FRIEND'S PHOTOS.` · then, large: `HOW FAR.`

segments.voice: Reread your first note. If you wrote anything down in the early days, a line, a list, a question, find it now, or when you can. If you didn't, take day one's line: someone is in there, say hi. Read it slowly. Then take one breath, the way you did at the bottom of the hill. Notice who is breathing now. Is anything different? Just notice. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Turning around on the path to see how far you've come, with curiosity, not a grade. Today's word.
Your line: how far. Once today, when you're climbing stairs or walking up a slope, stop and turn around. Look how far. Day three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Many traditions and many people mark the end of a season or year by looking back: rereading journals, reviewing the year's practice, and noticing what changed, without judgment.

Editor review 2026-10-01: rewrote the hook's opening ('if you've ever climbed... you know the moment' told listeners what they know); corrected 'a week from now' to six days; replaced 'in Latin and Greek, Hebrew and Sanskrit the word for breath and spirit started out as the same word' (an overstated etymology; Sanskrit prana is breath and life-force, not spirit) with 'in Latin, Greek and Hebrew one word can mean both' (spiritus, pneuma, ruach); tied the Kierkegaard line back to day 321 instead of reintroducing him.
